name: Sara Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. Your answers stay confidential. What is a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Sara Schmidt, 58, and I've built and repaired power lines since a vocational certificate and apprenticeship. I know the pump-station crossarms, like seeing a street light up after a repair, and use an approved AI assistant every day for fault photos and notes; I still check the wood and meter myself.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A hairline split on the shaded side of a warm crossarm looked clean in my first photograph. A second angle and our crew lead caught it before we loaded the wood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the AI assistant makes my fault notes easier to read, but it cannot smell a hot crossarm at the pump station. The field check still belongs to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a small change seems fine. I have a regular line wage, Nadia's insurance-claims job is steady today, and our savings cover about four months of bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep working the usual repair rota and use the approved AI assistant each night to sort photos and measurements from the day's faults. In the first year I'll keep checking its summaries against the signed isolation record and continue our normal savings payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm, though I still want to see what a tool misses. Our grown children have their own households, so evenings are quiet enough for me to review the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the tool miss at the pump station?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A warm crossarm had a hairline split on its shaded side, and my first photo looked normal. I took another angle and showed our crew lead the actual wood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the daily assistant make you trust it more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes me quicker at filing a question, not quicker at touching a line. The meter reading and the crew lead settle the job.

say: I'd say **AI notes** make repair records easier to read.
I'd insist **field checks** still find heat and damaged wood.
think: Our **four-month reserve** and two current wages make minor automation manageable.
I still watch for **missed physical faults** in any tool summary.
do: Keep the **usual repair rota** and sort fault photos with the approved assistant nightly.
Check **AI summaries** against signed isolation records and maintain normal savings payments.
feel: **Calm**, with curiosity about what the tool misses.
S0.quote: The meter reading and the crew lead settle the job.
fieldNote: Sara's **daily AI use** follows a real missed hairline split, prompting second-angle photographs and direct crew review.
A **four-month cushion** and Nadia's current claims income keep a quiet scenario financially manageable.

steps.text: Continue the usual paid repair rota and normal savings transfers
Use the approved assistant for nightly fault-photo notes checked against isolation records

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell managers to include claims staff, dispatchers and line crews in the tests before software changes staffing. A fast answer is useless if an address or a policy number is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My physical repairs should last for now, but Nadia checks insurance claims all day and that work could shrink quickly. Our four months saved give us time to adjust, yet a second wage is doing real work in our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll join the utility's approved route trial and record each wrong pump-station access point. In the first year Nadia would ask her employer about paid claims-review training, and we'd move her annual bonus to the emergency account rather than book the mountain trip until her hours settle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel excited about a tested route tool and anxious for Nadia's job. I don't want her experience reduced to a line of text in a manager's report.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which access point would you test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pump station has a north gate that stays locked during maintenance, while the east gate has the key box. A wrong route adds half an hour to an outage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could claims-review training protect Nadia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for a while, if a human still checks disputed cases, but I can't promise the role survives full thinking AI. She would ask for the actual pay and tasks before enrolling.

say: I'd seek **joint worker tests** before staffing changes in claims or dispatch.
I'd warn that **wrong access points** delay field repairs.
think: Nadia's **claims-checking hours** could shrink soon at the insurance office.
Our **four-month reserve** helps, but the second wage pays current bills.
do: Join the **approved route trial** and log pump-station gate errors.
Ask about **paid claims training** for Nadia and save her bonus instead of booking the mountain trip.
feel: **Excited** by field testing, anxious about Nadia's job.
S1.quote: A wrong route adds half an hour to an outage.
fieldNote: Sara sees **early household exposure** in Nadia's claims work while her own physical repairs still require people.
She uses a **gate-error log** and redirects an actual bonus to savings while paid training remains conditional.

steps.text: Use the approved route tool and log pump-station gate errors
Ask Nadia’s employer about paid claims-review training
Transfer Nadia’s annual bonus to emergency savings
Postpone the mountain trip until Nadia’s hours settle

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot thinking AI in 2028 could take Nadia's claims work first, and robots around 2031 could take repair calls. The union should demand published failure records and paid retraining before either group is cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 63 when robots can repair lines, and I could still need my wage. Nadia may already have lost claims hours; four months saved and some other utilities nearby help, but neither is a guaranteed replacement income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask our union branch for a worker-run robot trial and a paid inspection course. In 2029 I'd enroll if the utility covers wages and fees; when robots arrive in 2031 I'd apply for posted inspection roles here and nearby while keeping paid crew shifts if the depot offers them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious and determined. I'm quick to learn equipment. My enthusiasm cannot turn a trial badge into a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What failure would you publish?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether a robot notices the shaded split at the pump-station crossarm and stops before loading it. A success rate without missed cracks would mislead the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Nadia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Nadia we should budget as if her claims hours fall before my field hours do. Our grown children can help read vacancies, but their pay belongs to their own homes.

say: I'd separate **2028 claims AI** from 2031 field robots.
I'd demand **published failure records** and paid retraining through the union.
think: At **63**, I may still need line wages when robots arrive.
Nadia's **claims income** may shrink first, making four months saved a short bridge.
do: Ask the **union** for worker-run trials and a paid inspection course now.
Enroll if **fees and wages** are covered in 2029, then apply for posted inspection roles in 2031.
feel: **Anxious and determined**, without assuming a trial badge pays wages.
S2.quote: My enthusiasm cannot turn a trial badge into a wage.
fieldNote: Sara anticipates **two staggered income risks**, Nadia's thinking work in 2028 and her line repairs in 2031.
Her **robot trial criterion** is a shaded split missed by an earlier photo; training and vacancies remain conditional.

steps.text: Ask the union to negotiate worker-run trials and paid training
Enroll in inspection training in 2029 if fees and wages are covered
Apply for posted inspection roles at reachable utilities in 2031
Keep paid crew shifts during the inspection job search

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot five years gives workers time to test robots on the faults that diagrams hide. Thinking AI arrives in 2031 and field robots around 2034, when I'll be 66.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might retire at 66 if our written figures and a lower number for Nadia's claims income cover bills. If her job shrinks in 2031, I may need inspection pay in 2034 even with four months of savings today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll request retirement forecasts for us both and send the pump-station photo sequence to the union safety group. In 2032 I'd take a paid inspection placement if one opens; when robots arrive in 2034 I'd compare the posted wage with retirement income before choosing paid work or leaving the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more able to prepare, and less sure that a calendar alone will decide our retirement. We can test both the crossarm and our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the photo sequence show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first photograph looks clean; the side angle catches the split. I'd add the meter reading and date so another crew can repeat the check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop working at 66?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if Nadia and I can pay housing and medicine from actual income. I like field work, but I wouldn't stay just to prove a point to the machines.

say: I'd seek **hidden-fault trials** at the pump station before 2034 robot repairs.
I'd distinguish **2031 thinking AI** from later field robots.
think: Retirement at **66** depends on Nadia's lower-income case.
Four months of **savings** may not bridge a long claims-income cut.
do: Get **both retirement forecasts** and share verified pump-station photos this year.
Take a **paid placement** if offered in 2032; compare actual inspection pay with retirement in 2034.
feel: **More prepared**, uncertain whether retirement figures will work.
S3.quote: We can test both the crossarm and our budget.
fieldNote: Sara's **2034 decision** depends on Nadia's possibly reduced claims pay and real inspection wages, not an assumed age-based exit.
Her **side-angle photographs** provide a repeatable trial case rather than an unverified AI image.

steps.text: Compare written retirement forecasts with Nadia’s lower-income case
Submit checked pump-station photographs to the union safety group
Take a paid inspection placement in 2032 if offered
Apply for posted inspection work if retirement income falls short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger crews ten years is enough to make a library of faults the machines miss and give workers a say in the tests. Thinking AI arrives in 2036 and field robots around 2039, when I'll be 71.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect to have left climbing before 71 if our retirement statements cover housing and medicine. Nadia's claims work could change in 2036, so we should budget that risk before choosing a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep paid line shifts and update our household retirement budget each year. In 2037 Nadia and I would choose a date if lower claims income still covers bills; in 2039 I'd hand over the pump-station photographs to apprentices and join a union review if a robot misses that split.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my own field pay for the next few years and protective of the younger crew. A decade should leave them a record of real faults, not just clean demonstrations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you leave in the library?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shaded-side photograph, the first misleading image and the meter reading beside each other. An apprentice could see why a single clean photo is not enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the budget fails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep paid repair work if available and apply for an actual inspection opening. I wouldn't ask our grown children to finance a date we guessed wrong.

say: I'd build a **fault library** and ask workers to review robot trials.
I'd mark **2039 field robots** as the repair change when I'll be 71.
think: I may retire before **71** if written income covers housing and medicine.
Nadia's **claims pay** could fall in 2036, moving that date.
do: Keep **paid line shifts** and update the retirement budget annually.
Choose a **2037 date** if bills fit; hand apprentices pump-station photos and join a 2039 safety review.
feel: **Calm** about near-term wages, protective of younger crews.
S4.quote: An apprentice could see why a single clean photo is not enough.
fieldNote: Sara sees **2039 retirement** as plausible only after checking Nadia's earlier claims risk and written figures.
Her **fault library** pairs misleading and revealing images with a meter reading for future workers.

steps.text: Continue paid line shifts and update the household budget annually
Choose a 2037 retirement date only if lower claims pay covers bills
Join a 2039 union safety review if robots miss the pump-station split

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because Nadia's claims income could shrink before 2031 robots reach my repair work. Worker-run trials, paid inspection training, real local postings and clear household figures would help us make decisions.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who publishes the missed faults, not just the successful robot repairs. A photograph that looks clean can still hide a crack.

headlineQuote: A photograph that looks clean can still hide a crack.
portrait: Sara is a **58-year-old experienced lineworker** with a certificate and apprenticeship who uses approved AI tools daily for fault records.
Her **four-month reserve** support current stability, while Nadia's insurance-claims job faces thinking AI earlier.
She checks **physical wood and meters** after an AI-organized photograph missed a shaded crossarm split.
The **2031 robot date** worries her because her line repairs could change after Nadia's claims income shrinks.
A longer runway supports **worker-run trials** and retirement checks using a lower household-income case.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries Sara most because Nadia's claims income may fall before 2031 robots reach her repairs.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **worker-run trials**, paid inspection training, actual postings and clear retirement figures.
